 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Candidates Sprint to Finish in Campaign’s Final Hours
 President Trump, who has urged his supporters to pretend he is on the ballot, appeared to brace for the possibility of losses as Democrats expressed optimism they could flip control of Congress.
 Published Nov. 2, 2026 Updated Nov. 3, 2026, 12:47 a.m. ET Share full article

 Latest
 Pinned Ruth Igielnik Shawn McCreesh Patricia Mazzei and Callie Holtermann 
 Here’s the latest. 
 Candidates are making their last pitches in the final hours before Election Day, chasing votes in contentious midterm contests that will determine control of Congress. The outcome will likely hinge in part on how Americans feel about President Trump.
 Mr. Trump, who has for months sown mistrust in the electoral process, received an extraordinary rebuke on Monday night from the Supreme Court, which signaled in an unsigned order that it was not interested in assisting his efforts to interfere with how states administer elections. The court needed just a few hours to reject a request to require California to set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots that the administration claims have been provided to noncitizens.
 About 50 million Americans have already cast ballots, a surge of early voting that is outpacing the last midterms in every major Senate battleground. In several states, the share of the early vote from registered Democrats was higher than it was in 2024, an encouraging sign for the party as it seeks to flip control of Congress.
 A small number of races — including in unlikely battlegrounds like Maine, Kansas, South Carolina and Texas — are expected to determine which party controls the Senate for the rest of Mr. Trump’s presidency. In their rallies on Monday night, nominees in crucial races delivered messages of encouragement and exhaustion.
 James Talarico, a Democratic state legislator running for Senate , projected confidence in Austin, Texas, where he told supporters that Republicans are “terrified” that he will defeat Ken Paxton, the Republican state attorney general. Mr. Paxton, who won Mr. Trump’s endorsement, also made his final push to rally supporters on Monday. “Don’t wake up Wednesday wishing you’d done more,” he said on social media.
 Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina briefly addressed supporters at a brewery in Cayce, S.C. “As you can tell, my voice is gone, but I wasn’t going to miss this for anything,” she said. Her Democratic challenger, Dr. Annie Andrews, told supporters in Charleston that she was running mostly on “coffee, protein bars and giant Diet Cokes from gas stations.” She added, “Don’t tell my doctor!”
 Interviews with more than 28,000 voters conducted by The New York Times and Siena University revealed consistent themes : economic anxiety, the importance of individual candidates over party affiliation and Mr. Trump’s unpopularity.
 Mr. Trump, who has repeatedly urged supporters to pretend he is on the ballot, insisted that Republicans would win if his base turned out. But he also seemed prepared for the possibility of defeat. “For some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms,” Mr. Trump said, “but we gave this a very strong shot.”
 Democrats, energized by positive polls in several close races, expressed hope that reclaiming control of the Senate was possible. For weeks, surveys have indicated that voters’ frustration with the high cost of living has turned even deeply conservative states competitive, as Mr. Trump’s popularity has deteriorated.
 The latest Times/Siena polls, released on Sunday night, showed Democratic Senate candidates leading their Republican rivals in almost all seven major battleground states.
 Here’s what else to know:
 Election coverage: More than 400 Times reporters, editors, data analysts, video journalists and photographers have been covering the midterm elections, seeking to understand a large country with voters who are complicated — and sometimes contradictory. Read more › 
 Pre-emptive pardons: Mr. Trump told The New York Post that he was prepared to issue pre-emptive pardons for allies like Elon Musk and administration officials if Democrats were to take control of Congress and open investigations into their conduct. Read more › 
 Fears of vigilantism: As Mr. Trump keeps up his attack on the integrity of elections, local law enforcement and election officials across the country are preparing for possible threats or disruptions at polling sites. Read more › 
 Show more Nov. 2, 2026, 10:42 p.m. ET Zach Montague 
 Reporting from Washington
 A judge declines to halt D.H.S. demands for states to screen ballots. 
 Image A Los Angeles polling station on Monday. California is one of four states that have successfully used their constitutional authority to challenge the Trump administration’s claims of voter fraud. Credit... Etienne Laurent/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images A federal judge late on Monday turned down a request by Democratic lawmakers and party organizations to prohibit the Trump administration from coercing states into screening incoming ballots.
 The judge, James E. Boasberg of the Federal District Court for the District of Columbia, assessing the last-minute push by the Trump administration on the eve of the midterm elections to try to disqualify voters in a handful of Democratic-led states, wrote that states like California that were targeted had already largely succeeded in rebuffing the federal government.
 He added that until there were signs that states could not stop the Trump administration’s efforts “to dictate changes to their voting procedures,” the groups suing had not suffered any direct impacts that he could step in to correct.
 Judge Boasberg wrote that states were “hardly bit players” when it came to federal elections, and that the four targeted — California, Nevada, Washington and Pennsylvania — had successfully used their constitutional authority to challenge the Trump administration’s claims of voter fraud. When each received letters from the Homeland Security Department purportedly showing that they had allowed noncitizens to register to vote, each pushed back, demanding clearer evidence and declining to categorically remove voters the administration flagged.
 In court last week, the Justice Department said that states were free to ignore the letters from the Homeland Security Department altogether.
 Judge Boasberg wrote that it was not clear that just because a state had been threatened by the Trump administration, “officials there will capitulate to defendants’ entreaties.”
 As the Justice Department this month began to sue to force state officials to scrutinize voters based on the Homeland Security Department’s findings, he noted that federal judges had so far sided with the states.
 He pointed to his own ruling on Monday in a different case, in which he had blocked the Trump administration from intervening in California’s election. In that case, he found that the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, a group that assists recently naturalized citizens with voting, had been directly affected because its members appeared likely to have been misidentified as noncitizens by the federal government.
 The groups behind the lawsuit, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the Democratic Governors Association and the Nevada State Democratic Party, had argued that the Trump administration’s efforts could lead to Democratic voters being disenfranchised, harming their candidates in the midterm elections.
 Hours before the ruling, the Supreme Court also tersely declined to order California to set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots that the Trump administration had claimed, with minimal evidence, had been sent to noncitizens illegally registered to vote in the state.
 Judge Boasberg concluded that his calculus would have been different if state officials had given in to the Trump administration’s demands.
 Last week, he ordered the Trump administration to share the full list of states it had pursued with voter fraud claims, in case that included Republican-led states that might have quietly agreed to set aside ballots. The list was provided to the Democratic groups, but in a filing on Saturday, they argued that the Trump administration had not been forced to disclose which states might be “next on their list.”
 Judge Boasberg wrote that unless evidence emerged that the Trump administration was succeeding in compelling even one state to change its election protocols, he could not step in.
 “Had state officials capitulated in the face of the administration’s browbeating, this may well have been a different case,” he wrote. “At this stage in the litigation, however, plaintiffs present no evidence demonstrating that any state has acquiesced and removed a voter from the rolls or segregated her ballot based on the government’s letters.”

 Reporting from Iowa In an 890-word social media post titled “The Choices We Make,” Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan wrote that she was “troubled” by her fellow Democrats’ reaction to her last-minute endorsement of Michigan’s Republican Senate nominee, former Representative Mike Rogers. She rejected suggestions that Jason Turkish, her fiancé who endorsed Rogers on Wednesday, “must have made the decision for” her.
 “That is sexism dressed up as political analysis,” Stevens wrote. “My fiancé has his own views. I have mine. I made this decision, and I am proud of it. Do not question my independence simply because you disagree with my conclusion.”
 She also re-emphasized her frustration with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee, for not welcoming her into his campaign. “I put the party first and hoped we could move forward together,” she wrote of her endorsement of him after the primary. “Instead, I was shut out.”
 Nov. 2, 2026, 10:03 p.m. ET Erica L. Green 
 White House reporter President Trump wrapped up Election Day Eve with a brief interview with Sean Hannity on Fox News, where he ticked through his usual list of perceived accomplishments. But he continued to signal that he was ready to move on from the campaign and was prepared for tomorrow’s results to be disappointing. “I’m essentially shutting it down now — we’ll see,” said Trump. “We’ve had a great presidency. We’ve had a great two years.”
 Earlier in the day, during a speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, he spent roughly half of his remarks touting his renovation of the landmark, and other projects around Washington before lamenting that even though sitting presidents don’t usually win midterms, “we gave this a very strong shot.”
 Trump, who held dozens of rallies across the country in recent weeks, spent the rest of his day holding tele-rallies — he told Hannity he held a total of 15 — in several states, including Indiana, Alaska, Georgia, New York and Louisiana. The president is scheduled to stay in Washington on Tuesday, and will host an election night “viewing reception” in the East Room of the White House.
 Nov. 2, 2026, 9:57 p.m. ET Kellen Browning 
 Reporting from Eagle River, Alaska At an Election Day Eve event at a brewery outside Anchorage, Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska, a Republican, devoted the majority of his remarks to rehashing a New York Times article detailing how the campaign of his Democratic opponent, Mary Peltola, played a role in recruiting spoiler candidates, including another Dan Sullivan, onto the Senate ballot who might siphon votes away from him. President Trump has accused Democrats in Alaska of voter fraud. Senator Sullivan stopped short of accusing his opponent of illegal behavior, though he said he’d already met a handful of people who accidentally voted for the wrong Dan Sullivan.
 Image Credit... Erin Schaff/The New York Times Nov. 2, 2026, 9:51 p.m. ET J. David Goodman 
 Reporting from Texas A section of James Talarico’s closing message is focused on Elon Musk, who moved to Austin but whose name elicits loud boos from the crowd of Talarico supporters here.
 “In all likelihood, in all likelihood, if you’ve seen an attack ad on your TV, that was Elon,” Talarico said, referring to the more than $150 million spent by Musk to support Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate, and attack Talarico. “Ken Paxton is funded by one dude!”

They are terrified,” he says of Republicans who have spent hundreds of millions of dollars against him. “They see what we see —that we’re about to win this election tomorrow night.”

 Reporting from Iowa Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee for Senate in Iowa, completed her stump speech in Des Moines on Monday by claiming the country is at a pivotal moment. The crowd cheered with enthusiasm as Hinson hit her talking points, and rushed to sign her navy blue bus with a silver marker when she concluded her remarks.

 Reporting from Iowa “I’m not having a whole bunch of fun spending $70 every week on my 2014 Ford Taurus.”
 Gabrial Major, 21, who said he stood in line for two hours today to vote in Polk County, Iowa. Other than high fuel costs, his main concern was the high nitrate levels in the state’s waterways.
 Image Credit... Ann Hinga Klein for The New York Times Nov. 2, 2026, 8:42 p.m. ET J. David Goodman 
 Reporting from Texas I’m at James Talarico’s final rally in Austin, Texas, where he has packed an outdoor music venue for what is literally a rock concert. The Democratic Senate candidate has yet to take the stage, but there has already been plenty of live music and dancing. Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic state representative challenging Gov. Greg Abbott, is also slated to speak. There are good vibes but also a lot of nervousness. 
 “I feel cautiously optimistic,” said Leland Smith, 33. 
 “I feel nauseously optimistic,” his friend Corey Gayheart, 29, added.
 Video Credit Credit... J. David Goodman/The New York Times Advertisement

 Reporting from Charleston, S.C. Dr. Annie Andrews used her last campaign rally on Monday evening to encourage independent and Republican voters to do something unusual for Republican-leaning South Carolina and vote for a Democrat for the Senate.
 “We have more in common than Washington would like us to think,” she told hundreds of supporters gathered outdoors on a breezy night in her home of Charleston. Later, she added: “Let’s show Washington that South Carolina is not for sale.”
 Andrews, a pediatrician and mother of three, told the crowd that she was “about out of steam.” “I’m fueled mostly right now by coffee, protein bars and giant Diet Cokes from gas stations,” she said. “Don’t tell my doctor!”
 Image Credit... Win Mcnamee/Getty Images Nov. 2, 2026, 8:40 p.m. ET Callie Holtermann 
 Reporting from Cayce, S.C. Senator Darline Graham made her final pitch to voters at a brewery in Cayce, S.C., where supporters had gathered with pints of beer, rolls of stickers and their pet dogs. The pitch was brief — lasting less than two minutes — because Graham has almost completely lost her voice in the frenzied run-up to Election Day.
 “As you can tell, my voice is gone, but I wasn’t going to miss this for anything,” Graham said.
 There were whoops from the crowd when Tim Scott, the state’s senior senator, asked whether anyone had already voted. “I’m even calling my ugly cousins and taking them out to vote, because this election is too important to skip,” he said.
 Alan Wilson, the state’s attorney general and Republican nominee for governor, acknowledged that some voters were still feeling sore after Graham’s victory in a tight primary runoff. “Not everybody is happy with how the primary season ended, but the reality is, our party spoke, we nominated her, and I think she’s going to make an excellent United States senator,” he said.
 Image Credit... Allison Joyce/Getty Images Nov. 2, 2026, 8:33 p.m. ET Maya King 
 Reporting from Michigan Mike Rogers started his last stump speech before Election Day with lots of thank yous to his family and supporters. He tepidly broadcast confidence ahead of the vote count, saying he believed he would “surprise people” on Tuesday. He also shouted out the Democrats who have endorsed him, including the big one over the weekend.
 “Our Sunday wasn’t really planned to look like it was,” Rogers said of Representative Haley Stevens’s endorsement. “But someone else had enough courage to believe that country was more important than party.” He added that during church service on Sunday, Stevens leaned over to let him know she would be endorsing him.
 Image Credit... Victor J. Blue for The New York Times Nov. 2, 2026, 8:25 p.m. ET Beth Reinhard 
 Reporting from southern Maine This is the first time I’ve spent the eve of an election in a bowling alley. But it’s an on-brand venue for the Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson, a former Maine logger with blue-collar credentials. About 200 supporters are here, and Jackson is posing for photos and shaking hands. Oh, wait! He just bowled a spare. Bam!
 Image Credit... Kevin Lamarque/Reuters Advertisement
 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Nov. 2, 2026, 8:21 p.m. ET Zach Montague 
 A federal judge turned down a request from Democratic lawmakers and party organizations that he prohibit the Trump administration from coercing states into screening incoming ballots the way it had attempted to in California, or otherwise purging registered voters. Judge James E. Boasberg wrote that other courts had already intervened when the administration targeted specific states, and that the coalition had not been directly impacted in a way that gave them the right to sue.
 The Trump administration’s “attempted interference has yet to alter a single rule or process governing the upcoming election,” he wrote. “On the contrary, plaintiffs’ own pleadings establish that the states targeted by defendants have so far rebuffed the government’s efforts to dictate changes to their voting procedures.”
 Nov. 2, 2026, 8:16 p.m. ET Ishani Desai 
 Reporting from Iowa Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee for the Senate in Iowa, took a bus tour on Monday through three cities in Iowa. Her last stop is Des Moines tonight with her bus driving into an Airport Holiday Inn to the cheers of dozens. Chuck Grassley, who has represented Iowa in the Senate since 1981, joined her in Des Moines.
 Image Credit... Kamil Krzaczynski/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images Nov. 2, 2026, 8:12 p.m. ET Maya King 
 Reporting from Michigan Voters who say they were lifelong Democrats before this election are addressing the crowd at a rally for Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate, in suburban Detroit. One voter thanked Representative Haley Stevens, a Democrat, for her cross-party endorsement in her remarks, leading to chants of “Haley! Haley!” Stevens is not in attendance.
 Nov. 2, 2026, 8:08 p.m. ET Maya King 
 Reporting from Michigan John James, the Republican candidate for governor in Michigan, tried to deflect the attacks his party has received amid sinking approval ratings for President Trump. “At some point,” he said in his stump speech in Rochester Hills outside Detroit, “we have to look ourselves in the mirror and say that regardless of what party you’re in, we all get to vote for change.” 
 Advertisement
 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Nov. 2, 2026, 8:08 p.m. ET Heather Tal Murphy 
 “I want decency. I want courtesy. I want respect.”
 Kip Rusek, 69, voting almost entirely for Democrats in Helena, Montana on Monday. She said she felt strongly that Trump and other Republicans were being excessively cruel in their efforts to keep transgender women out of women’s bathrooms.
 Image Credit... Heather Murphy for The New York Times Nov. 2, 2026, 7:34 p.m. ET Mack Liederman 
 Reporting from Cleveland On the last stretch of the campaign trail, Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, has largely avoided speaking much about his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton, beyond criticizing her record as the state’s public health director during the Covid pandemic. Speeches on the campaign bus tour that I’ve heard from Ramaswamy and Senator Jon Husted have focused on cultural issues and socialism. They have made little to no mention of rising prices or the Iran war.
 “We’ll see if we deliver a surprise tomorrow,” Ramaswamy said to his audience in Cleveland. A most recent Times/Sienna poll shows him trailing in the race.
 Image Credit... Jon Cherry/Getty Images Image Credit... Jon Cherry/Getty Images Nov. 2, 2026, 7:23 p.m. ET Edgar Sandoval 
 I’m at a burger restaurant in San Antonio, where Greg Abbott, the Texas governor who is locked in a tough re-election fight, just held his last campaign event a day before Election Day. He spoke before a small but enthusiastic crowd that chanted “Four More Years!” He told the crowd that the this looks to be one of the most challenging elections of his career. Abbott has raised more than $200 million for his re-election campaign. His Democratic opponent, Gina Hinojosa, seemed to come out of nowhere after a quiet summer election season and is now locked in a tight race with him. Abbot hit a familiar note, accusing Ms. Hinojosa of being a typical liberal. “We have to keep Texas, Texas,” he told the crowd. “My opponent Gina Hinojosa wants to California my Texas.”
 Video Credit Credit... Edgar Sandoval/The New York Times Nov. 2, 2026, 7:23 p.m. ET Bethlehem Feleke and Jeremy Raff 
 Reporting from Texas “It was a struggle right up until the vote and honestly, even after the vote.”
 Brandon Balance, 46, voting early in Fort Worth, Texas, for the Republican Ken Paxton for Senate. He said he generally votes Republican and had misgivings about the bribery and fraud accusations that have trailed Paxton, but he’s hopeful the U.S. is on the right path with Republican leadership.
 Video Credit Credit... Jeremy Raff/The New York Times Advertisement
 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Nov. 2, 2026, 7:09 p.m. ET Tim Balk 
 Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, chair of Senate Democrats’ campaign arm, brushed off Representative Haley Stevens’s decision to endorse Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan. “I don’t think voters are going to care, because they’re focused on the price of gasoline,” Gillibrand said in an interview today, expressing confidence in the chances of Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, who narrowly defeated Stevens in an August primary. “Abdul El-Sayed has run such a strong campaign exciting new voters across the state of Michigan.” Gillibrand also said she had not known “anything about” an effort by Democrats to stack Alaska’s ballot for Senate .
 Nov. 2, 2026, 7:07 p.m. ET Callie Holtermann 
 Reporting from Cayce, S.C. On Fox News, Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina urged the state’s Republican voters not to write in any other candidate’s name in her tight Senate race. Graham’s bid for a full term has been complicated by a write-in campaign organized by supporters of her primary opponent, Representative Ralph Norman. “I’m the only conservative on the ballot, so if you skip over me, or if you do a write-in, it’s going to be a vote for Annie Andrews,” she said, referring to the Democratic nominee.
 Then Graham was off to a final rally at a brewery in Cayce, S.C., where a band played “Don’t Stop Believin’” to send off the Republican slate of candidates.

 The Justice Department charges more people with voter fraud in California. 
 Image Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, center, announced that six people were charged with having illegally voted in the 2024 election. Credit... Jae C. Hong/Associated Press Federal prosecutors on Monday charged another six people in California with having illegally voted in the 2024 presidential election, the latest move in the Trump administration’s effort to identify and publicize instances of voter fraud.
 The charges, announced on Monday by the Justice Department, come amid the administration’s efforts to segregate some 20,000 California ballots that it claims were cast by “likely noncitizens” — an assertion that state election officials have firmly rejected. Judges have rejected the federal government’s arguments in a series of rulings over the last 10 days, including on Monday at the Supreme Court in an unsigned order.
 At a news conference on Monday, Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, said that the six charged, in addition to the 28 charged last month, were among the 20,000. More than 230 people across 28 states have been charged in connection with voting violations during President Trump’s second term.
 “Voting is the essence of American citizenship,” Mr. Essayli said at the news conference. “Illegally attempting to infiltrate and influence our political determinations is not only wrong; it’s a crime.”
 Also on Monday, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., granted a preliminary injunction that blocked the federal government from pressuring California officials to segregate the ballots, describing the lists as “flawed” and noting that the administration did not have the authority to do so.
 “California may decide for itself what procedures to use for verifying the citizenship of registered voters and for deciding whether to count their mail-in ballots,” wrote Chief Judge James E. Boasberg, noting that the executive branch lacked the authority to “unilaterally impose its preferred procedures.”
 Election officials in California and other states have condemned the federal government’s crackdown, saying its system for identifying suspected violators is flawed and based on incomplete information.
 At the news conference on Monday, Mr. Essayli said that federal authorities planned to move forward with criminal prosecutions and were enlisting the help of some local California authorities to do so.
 In addition to the federal cases, one person was charged with illegally registering to vote and voting in San Luis Obispo, Calif., the city’s district attorney, Dan Dow, said at the news conference.
 He said his office was close to making decisions on 16 other similar cases.
 “When a person who is not a citizen casts a ballot, a foreign national is making a decision that only belongs with Americans,” Mr. Dow said.

 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Nov. 2, 2026, 6:07 p.m. ET Shawn McCreesh 
 Reporting from the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool
 Trump delivers a closing midterm message. Mostly about landscaping. 
 Image “The pipes now are totally renovated,” President Trump said as he showed off the newly refilled Reflecting Pool on Monday. Credit... Doug Mills/The New York Times President Trump was standing in front of the Reflecting Pool on Monday afternoon, doing a little reflecting of his own.
 “For some reason,” he was saying, the Washington Monument mirrored in the newly reopened pool behind him, “the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms. But we gave this a very strong shot.”
 It was the day before the election, and the president had decided to come here, a place that excites him, to talk about many of the topics that make him happiest. Trouble is, almost none of those topics have anything to do with the issues that are driving this election.
 At a time when voters have made clear they’re most concerned with the high prices of gas and groceries and a new war in the Middle East, Mr. Trump used his final in-person appearance before Americans head to the polls to talk about drain pipes, top soil, limestone, fountains and his favorite kind of columns.
 “The pipes now are totally renovated,” Mr. Trump said. Propped up next to him was a poster board showing an aerial view of the pool, with this caption: “Back, and more beautiful than ever!”
 The “brand-new pipes,” Mr. Trump said, are “very important in terms of the algae and other things. And it’s a complete job, and we’re very proud of it.”
 The Lincoln Memorial in front of him, Mr. Trump addressed a small audience seated in folding chairs. There were a few dozen National Park Service employees, reporters, White House officials and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. At one point early in his speech, Mr. Trump beckoned to a young man who bounded up onstage with a stack of large printouts under his arm.
 “Great,” Mr. Trump said as he took the stack and began rifling through it. He held up one of the printouts. It was a photograph of what looked like a rusty drainpipe. Another photograph showed a dumpster filled with detritus.
 “This is another example of what it looked like just at water level and below,” he explained as he waved another photograph aloft. Every so often, he would look over his shoulder to check on the body of water behind him. “It’s a massive piece of pool,” he said, sounding impressed. It looked clean, dark and choppy on this early November day.
 The Reflecting Pool had been closed and fenced off since July. After a series of bungled repair jobs , it became a symbol of the Trump administration’s dysfunction.
 After he finished with the pictures, the president turned to other matters of national interest. Matters including: the nature of Corinthian columns (“the most beautiful in the world”); the soul of grass generally, and Bermuda grass specifically (“like the human being, grass has a life also”); the endurance of granite (“it literally has thousands of years of life”); the renovation of a public golf course on the Potomac that he’s planning; statues; the White House ballroom; graffiti; and the new White House helipad. 
 “The helipad,” Mr. Trump said, “was desperately needed.”
 In the history of American politics, the speech may go down as one of the more unusual closing messages on the eve of an election. But it was a pretty good crystallization of what matters to Mr. Trump as he heads into the lame duck phase of his second term — despite, or maybe because of, his depressed poll numbers and voter unhappiness over the economy, corruption and an unresolved war.
 And now here he was, using his final in-person address before the election to talk more about his chryselephantine fantasies of ballrooms and arches and Corinthian columns.
 “The president’s a builder,” Mr. Burgum said from the little stage on Monday. “You can’t keep him away!” Large signs that aides had duct-taped to the stage before the president’s arrival read: “RESTORING OUR CAPITAL.”
 The president made some of his usual comments about the war with Iran, the U.S. economy and various culture war issues, but he did not even attempt to explain how any of the renovation projects that were the focus of the speech related to any of the issues animating the midterm elections.
 “I’ve traveled all across the country, spoken at all of these rallies I’ve done over the last two and a half weeks,” he said. “America is ready to go. They’re ready to vote. I hope they’re ready to do the right thing.”
 It seemed almost as though he had run out of things to say about politics and governance, and like he simply wanted to talk about what sparks joy for him.
 “We have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation,” Mr. Trump said, “but for that you don’t have enough time.”

 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Nov. 2, 2026, 5:05 p.m. ET Zolan Kanno-Youngs 
 Zolan Kanno-Youngs, who covers the White House, has been chronicling President Trump’s efforts to reshape the rules governing elections.
 Trump’s election fraud reward offer raises fears of vigilantism among local officials. 
 Image Early voting in Anchorage on Sunday. President Trump has offered a $1 million reward for information leading to an election fraud conviction. Credit... Erin Schaff/The New York Times Local law enforcement and election officials are bracing for a tense Election Day as President Trump has kept up a sustained attack on the integrity of U.S. elections, including by offering a $1 million reward for information that leads to an election fraud conviction.
 In response to Mr. Trump’s unsubstantiated claims about voting problems and his campaign to assert more federal control over state-run elections, officials have prepared for potential worst-case scenarios in which the federal government tries to intervene in voting.
 Now some local authorities have said they also fear that the president’s offer of a large financial incentive could foster unrest or even vigilantism, with Americans eying one another with suspicion as they head to the polls.
 “Don’t drag in the public and basically a vigilante-type system where we’re going to say, ‘Hey, you can make a million dollars here by going over here and accusing somebody of fraud,’” said Sheriff Chris Nanos of Pima County, Ariz., a Democrat. “Our elections are handled at the local level, but yet we have fire and brimstone, if you will, coming down from the federal level.”
 Mr. Trump’s unfounded claims that the election could be rigged come at a time when violent threats against public officials and election workers have increasingly become a new normal. To prepare for Tuesday, election officials and local law enforcement agencies have held hundreds of exercises to anticipate a variety of possible threats and disruptions at polling sites.
 Image In the final stretch of the midterm campaign, Mr. Trump has continued to make unsubstantiated claims that the country’s elections can be manipulated. Credit... Doug Mills/The New York Times Chief Chris Davis, who leads the police department in Green Bay, Wis., said the level of fear surrounding elections has increased in recent years, particularly in his battleground state.
 “I worry about disturbances at polling places, and we’ve developed pretty comprehensive plans for that if it happens,” said Chief Davis, who added that he was concerned Mr. Trump’s reward offer could further heighten tensions at polling sites.
 “If one voter challenges another voter, the potential for that to turn into a disturbance and a big problem for us is very real,” he said.
 Deidre Henderson, the Republican lieutenant governor of Utah, has also warned in recent weeks that the federal government has contributed to a tense environment for the midterms.
 Ms. Henderson told CBS News’s “60 Minutes” that in previous elections, “the threats were all external: nonstate actors, cybersecurity threats and other things. But now we also have threats coming from within our own government.”
 The atmosphere is already fraught. The Justice Department has asked California to set aside 20,000 mail ballots, claiming they were provided to likely noncitizens. The administration has also sought to pre-emptively challenge the results of the Senate race in Alaska, where two candidates named Dan Sullivan are on the ballot. So far, the courts have blocked those efforts.
 State and local officials have responded to Mr. Trump’s attacks by seeking to create guardrails to prevent potential disruptions.
 Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, a Democrat, sent an extraordinary “alert” on Saturday to the four U.S. district courts that cover California, warning the judges that the Trump administration may try to seize ballots.
 And in response to the Justice Department’s plan to dispatch 1,000 federal monitors across the country, some local officials have issued statements saying that monitors are prohibited from crossing into an established perimeter surrounding polling locations, citing state law.
 Image Early voting in Miami on Friday. A Justice Department spokeswoman said that election monitors are trained to follow local laws that govern access at polling sites. Credit... Ruth Fremson/The New York Times Justin Elicker, the Democratic mayor of New Haven, Conn., said the Justice Department told local officials last month that it would be sending two teams of two people to polling sites in the city to ensure New Haven was complying with federal voting requirements on language assistance and disability access.
 The city responded by sending the Justice Department a letter saying the monitors were not welcome to enter any polling locations.
 “They intimidate people not to vote,” Mr. Elicker said in an interview. “We would prefer that they not be here.”
 In discussions with local and state officials, the Justice Department committed to monitoring from outside a 75-foot perimeter, like other observers, and pledged not to interfere with voting, according to Stephanie Thomas, Connecticut’s Democratic secretary of the state.
 A Justice Department spokeswoman said federal monitors do not require approval from state or local authorities but added that monitors are trained to follow local laws that govern access at polling sites.
 In the final stretch of the midterm campaign, Mr. Trump has continued to make unsubstantiated claims that the country’s elections can be manipulated, falsely asserting that there is widespread fraud.
 “I’m also going to be issuing a $1 million bonus or reward, or whatever you want to call it, for anybody that reports voter fraud, leading to the arrest and conviction of somebody,” Mr. Trump told reporters last week before flying to Mississippi for a campaign rally.
 The president has said the offer applies to past elections, as well as the midterms.
 Mr. Trump’s dangling of a $1 million reward caps a year in which he has trained the full arsenal of his administration on sowing doubt about the country’s election systems.
 The White House declined to answer questions about what money would be used to pay for the reward or how Americans should report fraud, and did not address criticism that the financial incentive could spur people to vigilantism.
 Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said that Democrats were the ones eroding election security. “They refused to enact common-sense election security measures like voter ID and citizenship verification,” she said in a statement. “President Trump is right: We have to have honest elections.”
 Despite the inflamed rhetoric, local and state officials said that the authorities tasked with ensuring a safe election are prepared for this moment.
 “A lot of what has been said has been designed to provoke and cause fear, so we’re paying attention to it but we’re not going to overreact,” said Aghogho Edevbie, the deputy secretary of state of Michigan, who said that his office has helped conduct about 125 security exercises this cycle.
 “That is going to cause us to be ready for anything that comes along,” said Mr. Edevbie, a Democrat. “You could ask, ‘Was that more preparation because of what’s happening from D.C.?’ Absolutely.”
 Gowri Ramachandran, the director of elections and security in the Brennan Center’s Elections and Government Program, said Americans should not lose faith in poll workers.
 “Election officials just really have been working super hard to provide a free and fair election for voters,” Ms. Ramachandran said. “The rhetoric that we see coming out of the administration just does not square with the reality of what election officials and voters are doing. And I would say the only way all of that rhetoric works is if people don’t exercise their rights to vote.”
 Nearly three-quarters of voters said they largely trusted that the results of Tuesday’s election would be accurate, including large majorities of Democrats, Republicans and independents, according to a recent New York Times/Siena poll . Still, half of likely voters were worried about Republicans trying to overturn the outcome of the election, while 31 percent of voters were worried about the possibility of Democrats taking such action.
 Chuck Wexler, the executive director of the Police Executive Research Forum, which advises departments on best practices, said that current and former police chiefs discussed at a recent gathering how the political divisiveness at the national level had trickled down to communities trying to prepare for the election.
 “There are some people who are willing to go beyond rhetoric to actual exercise violence, and that has not been lost on police chiefs,” Mr. Wexler said, noting the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the U.S. Capitol by supporters of Mr. Trump who were angry about the outcome of the 2020 election. “What used to be a simple constitutional right of voting now has become an issue of considerable agitation.”
 Neil Vigdor , Devlin Barrett and Eileen Sullivan contributed reporting.

 Georgia Democrats fear state races could be close enough to set off disruptive hand counts. 
 Image An early voting site in Atlanta in October. Georgia state law requires a manual recount of all ballots in a host of state races if the results of the initial tally are within 0.5 percent. Credit... Erik S. Lesser/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images In Georgia, Democrats expecting Senator Jon Ossoff to win his re-election bid are also cautiously optimistic about their slate of down-ballot candidates. But some Democrats are also worried about potential delays, or even chaos, if races for state offices end up so close that they trigger automatic statewide hand recounts under a law signed earlier this year.
 The law , drafted in a special session of the Republican-controlled State Legislature, requires Georgia’s secretary of state to direct a manual recount of all ballots in a race if the results of the initial tally are within 0.5 percent. The law applies to races for governor, lieutenant governor and a host of other state offices. It does not apply to races for the U.S. Senate or House.
 On Monday, a Georgia state representative, Saira Draper, a Democrat, said that behind the scenes during the special session, Republican lawmakers had offered assurances that “a half-point race was a remote possibility — the vote was about placating election deniers, not about accuracy.”
 Now, she said, the possibility did not seem so remote. “If a hand recount is triggered, Georgians will be waiting on a slower, messier process that Republicans chose for political reasons, and they’ll own every bit of the chaos that comes with it,” she said.
 In 2020, Georgia carried out a manual recount of the close race between President Trump and Joseph R. Biden Jr. That recount was completed without major incident, and reduced Mr. Biden’s lead by 1,200 votes. Mr. Biden ended up narrowly winning the presidency, despite Mr. Trump’s unfounded allegations that the system was rigged against him.
 Officials this week in the office of Brad Raffensperger, the Republican secretary of state since 2019, said they were confident that the system was ready for a hand recount. “Georgia is prepared,” Blake Evans, the state elections director, said in a statement.

 A mysterious group is spending millions to boost third-party spoilers who could siphon Republican votes. 
 About $6.5 million has been spent over the final 10 days of the campaign on mailers and digital ads promoting obscure third-party candidates with almost no chance of winning on Tuesday. What gives?
 The material is an apparent “spoiler” effort to persuade voters who are considering backing a Republican to instead support right-wing candidates who would peel away votes from a major party nominee. The final days of campaigns often feature tactics like these, with the belief that futzing around on the margins of a race could be decisive in determining the ultimate winner.
 Mailers shared with The New York Times by Mintt, a mail-tracking firm, show some of the subterfuge that appears to be at play from a super PAC called Our Heritage Matters. The PAC was registered on Oct. 15, meaning it is not required to disclose its donors until December. All of its spending has been through two Delaware limited-liability companies that themselves were formed within the last month, on Oct. 6, and have reported no other activity, according to corporate records.
 In one of America’s tightest House races in Colorado, a mailer promoting Dave Wood, the Libertarian nominee, says that Representative Gabe Evans, a Republican, has a “liberal agenda” and would “join forces with Socialist Democrats.”
 Image Mintt, a mail-tracking firm, released an image of a mailer a super PAC called Our Heritage Matters sent to voters in Colorado that portrays Representative Gabe Evans, a Republican, as a Democrat. Credit... via Mintt A nearly identical mailer interchanges those names with the Republican nominee, Jennifer Balkcom, and the Libertarian candidate, Travis Groo, in North Carolina’s 11th District.
 Image Voters in North Carolina’s 11th District received a nearly identical mailer from Our Heritage Matters accusing the Republican nominee, Jennifer Balkcom, of having a “liberal agenda” and promoting the Libertarian candidate, Travis Groo. Credit... via Mintt Our Heritage Matters is also spending to influence voters in Senate races. Michele Tafoya, the Republican nominee for Senate in Minnesota, is also accused of having a “liberal agenda.” Another mailer from the group calls Mark Hackett, the Constitution Party candidate for Senate in South Carolina, “the true conservative” in the race.
 Image Another of the group’s mailers similarly attacks Michele Tafoya, the Republican nominee for Senate in Minnesota, and promotes her Libertarian opponent, Rebecca Whiting. Credit... via Mintt On its website, Our Heritage Matters says: “American culture, values, and traditions are worth defending. We stand for the principles that built this nation — and we will not stand by while they are eroded by enemies foreign and domestic.”
 The group did not respond to a request for comment.
